book.title: Sefer Soḳolḳah = Dos bukh fun Soḳolḳe (ʻa.y. Irgun Yotsʼe Soḳolḳah be-Yiśraʼel)

overview.title: Reading Jewish Sokółka through Sefer Sokolkah
overview.summary: Sefer Sokolkah presents Sokółka as a substantial Jewish community whose life was shaped by religious learning, schools, trades, families, political movements, and cultural activity [mention_01767cdae3927d939c1e01f5]. The memorial book follows that life through war, German occupation, ghettoization, deportation, murder, and the efforts of survivors and emigrants to preserve its memory [event_candidate_6048c3dc2707e61108e4f17b; event_candidate_8eb68a5070b14963def4791c; event_candidate_2b0f919e22ce93b2b48d607e]. Exploring these paths will help readers understand both the institutions that sustained Jewish life and the people whose testimony records persecution, resistance, survival, and loss. It also shows how Sokółka continued as a place of family memory through memorial gatherings, monuments, aid societies, and the memorial book itself [mention_8bbfaeb35dd71b13691fa69b; mention_3ad2bb8a5b719856a; mention_f0db7ef909b85dc05a6505d9].

paths.title: What kind of Jewish community was Sokółka?
paths.description: This path reconstructs Sokółka as a lived community: a town with religious institutions, schools, businesses, civic organizations, and closely connected families. By the end, readers will see the community as more than a demographic category or a place later defined by destruction [mention_068bb5fef3f539ffa57fe8ab; mention_a8dbacf6953013beab0949a2].
paths.question: How did Jewish residents build everyday communal life?

steps.title: A substantial and connected town
steps.summary: The memorial-book account portrays Sokółka as a town of about 20,000 inhabitants, including about 10,000 Jews, with institutions, societies, artists, and businesses. This scale helps explain why the community had a dense social world rather than a single communal center [mention_01767cdae3927d939c1e01f5; mention_068bb5fef3f539ffa57fe8ab].

steps.title: Religious learning and authority
steps.summary: Jewish education included several Talmud Torah settings, including an institution serving children from Sokółka and its surroundings. Rabbis and teachers such as Tzvi Hirsch Director and Chaim Meir Shmul connected learning, religious leadership, and communal continuity [mention_cc0f12b563459ff92f1a4af2; mention_aa05f15ce5e663820e60f6ea; mention_a1c1a1a87e9c82e965c42ee0].

steps.title: Work, commerce, and mutual support
steps.summary: Jewish livelihoods included tanning, leatherwork, milling, wholesale trade, and food businesses; seventeen tanneries alone had employed hundreds of Jewish workers. The book also records a local relief office and a cooperative loan-and-savings fund, showing how economic life was tied to communal assistance [mention_3573785c0e0a32770c520910; event_candidate_206e264dbaa20581a80f337f; event_candidate_a189fa9373d27d80a97a6945].

steps.title: Families and shared memory
steps.summary: The memorial book follows named families, including the Kantors, Shteins, and Goldackers, linking personal histories to Sokółka’s wider story. Such family entries preserve relationships, occupations, migration, and the consequences of destruction at an individual scale [mention_62058d5b8cf98031c5809bc5; mention_36b27203f2901b0138f26ac5; mention_d98bd65aecb21a4b87641864].

paths.title: How did education, culture, and politics shape Jewish identity?
paths.description: This path traces competing and overlapping forms of Jewish belonging: traditional study, modern Hebrew education, Zionism, Bundism, youth movements, and performance. It shows how Sokółka’s young people and educators debated the future while remaining rooted in communal institutions [mention_24f5bb3b243810080f05ac4f; mention_4d171184e5d2acf69888398c].
paths.question: What futures did Sokółka’s Jews imagine before the Holocaust?

steps.title: Traditional and modern schooling
steps.summary: Alongside the Talmud Torah, Sokółka developed Hebrew education: a reformed heder was attempted in 1903, and a Zionist group founded a Hebrew school in 1904–1905. These efforts show education becoming a meeting point between religious tradition and modern Jewish national culture [event_candidate_7cb346c07f8d74954ea73529; event_candidate_bf1278434abd3fb7957a1722].

records.title: Opening of a reformed heder
records.summary: In 1903 in Sokolka, a Hebrew teacher opened a reformed heder, but it did not continue for lack of students; the teacher's name is unclear.

steps.title: Political and Zionist debate
steps.summary: The book records Sokółka Jews participating in elections to four Dumas and later organizing around Zionist and Bundist ideas. Youth were drawn both toward Zionism and toward the Bund, revealing political disagreement within an active Jewish public sphere [event_candidate_3275ea09abea2510b7589c88; mention_24f5bb3b243810080f05ac4f; mention_db346d5e4d103cff043e3bd7].

steps.title: Youth movements and migration
steps.summary: After the First World War, the Land of Israel Office organized youth groups for immigration, and Hechalutz arose in Sokółka in 1919–1920. Many pioneers later left the town for the Land of Israel during the 1920s, turning political ideals into migration and collective work [event_candidate_e064a973a3e38a23ac1ac0ee; event_candidate_88a0eae934775b9f468ac00d; event_candidate_b8f5de7d17775e516342ea93].

steps.title: Culture as communal expression
steps.summary: Schoolchildren performed plays including Hannah and Her Seven Sons and The Sale of Joseph, while Sokółka’s Culture dramatic troupe presented The Verdict. These performances show children and adults using Hebrew and Yiddish culture to teach, entertain, and express collective concerns [mention_3f75ea85bbd3cec7830a147b; mention_8997609ce61cec4b0644ef6d; mention_eb905676dd3d4a2075bfb82a].

paths.title: How did occupation transform everyday life?
paths.description: This path follows the transition from invasion to forced administration, ghettoization, labor, and confinement. It helps readers understand how persecution dismantled ordinary institutions while exploiting Jewish labor and placing communal survival under coercive control [event_candidate_6048c3dc2707e61108e4f17b; event_candidate_555f9869c03a33791ce836d2].
paths.question: How did German rule change Sokółka before the deportations?

steps.title: Invasion and the first violence
steps.summary: German forces entered Sokółka at the beginning of September 1939. A later account describes German forces expelling Jews and desecrating Torah scrolls at the new study house, showing that occupation attacked both people and religious symbols [event_candidate_6048c3dc2707e61108e4f17b; event_candidate_3819d4c23cf669522e5fd77e].

records.title: German entry into Sokolka

steps.title: Forced administration and the ghetto
steps.summary: In 1941, a Judenrat was chosen under Attorney Friedberg, while authorities ordered a ghetto across three designated areas. These arrangements imposed German control through both spatial confinement and a council compelled to deal with the occupying authorities [event_candidate_a051169214d5df51af5314fb; event_candidate_555f9869c03a33791ce836d2].

steps.title: Labor under persecution
steps.summary: Jewish workers were confined in factories and forced into production, including leather work and military-related orders. The accounts of the fur factory, shoe workshop, felt factory, and Chaim Berlshtein’s leather workshop show how labor became part of the machinery of persecution [mention_757da75582a9712342b055bb; mention_37bfa4039bdada2a8e83f143; mention_9625c70500437f4c2be0d738].

steps.title: Transfer to camps
steps.summary: After the ghetto period, most prisoners were transferred to Kolbassin. The forced movement away from Sokółka marked a further loss of place, family connection, and control over one’s fate [event_candidate_65a3405b6c0b374d12cd31f2].

records.title: Transfer to Kolbassin
records.summary: Most prisoners were transferred to Kolbassin after the ghetto existed until 1942.

paths.title: What happened to Sokółka’s Jews, and where do we see resistance?
paths.description: This path follows the destruction of the community while preserving the evidence of escape, aid, underground activity, and individual survival. It makes clear that deportation and murder were processes, not a single event, and that people continued to act within extreme danger [event_candidate_50eaf8c5c86be387ae903e0b; event_candidate_06730164adf98f1d8880b5ac].
paths.question: How did destruction unfold, and how did people respond?

steps.title: Liquidation and deportation
steps.summary: In mid-October 1942, residents were assembled and selected; in early December, the Jews of Sokółka were gathered for transport toward Treblinka. The testimony places these actions within the organized destruction of the community rather than treating them as an isolated disappearance [event_candidate_8eb68a5070b14963def4791c; event_candidate_50eaf8c5c86be387ae903e0b].

records.title: Ghetto liquidation and deportation

records.title: Deportation of Sokolka Jews to Treblinka
records.summary: Sokolka Jews were assembled and deported toward Treblinka in early December 1942.

steps.title: Murder and the final transports
steps.summary: The deportees were reportedly murdered in early January 1943. Remaining ghetto prisoners were then taken under guard to the railway and transported to Auschwitz, where most were sent to gas chambers; a group of thirty-three young women was initially separated [event_candidate_06730164adf98f1d8880b5ac; event_candidate_7d17a9f55afbede0eeea5068; event_candidate_2b0f919e22ce93b2b48d607e].

steps.title: Escape, aid, and hiding
steps.summary: About twenty-five people were taken from the ghetto to Białystok through the efforts of a doctor, while refugees from Sokółka and Krinek later jumped from a train. Another testimony recalls a rural family hiding a Jewish child and being executed after the child was discovered [event_candidate_dc8fe216c9f205bcecfc13bb; event_candidate_4b18bc7a026dfd4361ed0083; mention_a9d9598726e09f5d695c9d78].

steps.title: Underground resistance and survival
steps.summary: Yitzhak Galdshteyn, born in Sokółka in 1916, is remembered as a member of HaNoar HaTzioni and an underground activist; the book reports that he died in the Warsaw bunker explosion. Abraham Kantarovsky’s account, by contrast, preserves a survivor’s escape from Auschwitz, showing different wartime paths within the same community’s story [mention_d2534079b95c4085f1c8629e; mention_729bb202fd7800321293ea7b; mention_7f6265cd088b67e93b9a5824].

paths.title: How did Sokółka survive in memory after the Holocaust?
paths.description: This path follows survivors and emigrants as they carried Sokółka into new places and created forms of remembrance. Readers will understand memory as an active communal responsibility: naming the dead, supporting survivors, building monuments, and preserving testimony [mention_fdad3a14288e7c463b43e206; mention_68f1a3cd1df00c16c7051555].
paths.question: What remained of Sokółka, and who carried its memory forward?

steps.title: A shattered family world
steps.summary: One testimony states that the narrator and Benjamin were the two surviving brothers of their entire family. Another describes the Shtein family as surviving the destruction through only a few descendants, making demographic loss visible through family experience [mention_fdad3a14288e7c463b43e206; mention_5809ef72a7666fb7f2c0cb6a].

steps.title: Return to an emptied hometown
steps.summary: After the war, a return journey recorded on 7 July 1946 found no Jews. The absence encountered by returning Sokolkers conveys the destruction of communal life more directly than numbers alone [event_candidate_1dd28496b56090f2d1262d07].

records.title: Return journey to Sokolka
records.summary: The narrator traveled together on July 7, 1946, and unfortunately found no Jews; Sokolka is not stated in the supplied quote.

steps.title: Landsleit rebuilding community
steps.summary: The Sokolker Aid Society organized support among landsmen, including projects in Israel and a United Jewish Appeal campaign, and planned an annual banquet in 1957. These activities show survivors and emigrants maintaining social responsibility across distance [mention_68f1a3cd1df00c16c7051555; mention_f0db7ef909b85dc05a6505d9; event_candidate_778241aa6ca5ff583860cbf3].

steps.title: Monument and memorial book
steps.summary: Sokółka landsleit established a memorial in Jerusalem for the town’s martyrs and planned a yizkor book to preserve the community’s history for future generations. Sefer Sokolkah therefore functions not only as a record of loss but also as an act of rebuilding communal presence through testimony [mention_3ad2bb8a5b71997372eb403; mention_7d062f5dc91d3defaf63ed0c; mention_ba368c4c63667c11189f7772].

timeline.dateLabel: First World War and its aftermath
timeline.title: War, displacement, and new movements
timeline.summary: The First World War disrupted plans for immigration, while the Russian retreat, the German advance, and later political changes reshaped Sokółka. After the war, youth groups organized for immigration to the Land of Israel [event_candidate_e60e0e5c3186d9cb99e5df73; event_candidate_382f0035eb563115516490f2; event_candidate_e064a973a3e38a23ac1ac0ee].
